newsitem.title: USA: British Air unveils expansion plan.
newsitem.headline: British Air unveils expansion plan.

text.p: British Airways Plc unveiled a three-year expansion plan Tuesday that will include new routes, services and ethnic artwork painted on its planes.

Britain's largest airline announced at news conferences in New York and London that it plans to spend hundreds of millions of dollars developing the new routes and a new approach to customer service over the next three years.

It also said it wanted to update its corporate image and become more global, while stressing the British Airways brand. The new corporate images, to grace the tailfins on more than 300 planes, will include 50 designs by local artists from South Africa, England and a host of other countries.
The carrier also reiterated plans to add 43 new aircraft to its fleet over the next three years: 29 Boeing 747-400s, nine 777s and five 757s.
British Airways Chairman Sir Colin Marshall said he was surprised, at first, at the suggestion to paint the fleet in a variety of designs.

"I supposed initially, the immediate reaction was one of surprise. But once one got a better impression of what was intended, I think it's a very striking approach to take," he said at the New York news conference.
The cost of redesigning and marketing the new corporate image was expected to be about $100 million, officials said. Some of that would have been spent anyway on repainting planes.

The facelift is the first overhaul since BA swapped the national flag for its sombre livery of dark blue, red and grey in 1984, when the British government was preparing to sell the airline in one of many privatisations under the Thatcher regime.

"Our existing livery has served us well. It helped us transform our company in preparation for privatisation," Chief Executive Robert Ayling said in London. "Now all of our research is telling us we must change again."
"Airlines are extraordinarily (nationally) chauvinistic companies," he told reporters. "And, I think, with more deregulation in the world they have to become more cosmopolitan."
Ayling said the changes had not been discussed with American Airlines, since BA's proposed alliance with American has not been approved by regulators.

In New York, Marshall said the airline had no idea when the proposed alliance might be approved. He reiterated BA's stance that it may forego the proposed alliance if regulators were to require the airlines to pay a burdensome price.

"We have always said that if the regulatory costs are going to be too great, we're going to have to give serious consideration to walking away. But we certainly hope that this is not going to be the case," Marshall said. The alliance is being studied by British, U.S. and European regulators.
Other highlights of the plan include:
-- more partnerships along the lines of the proposed alliance with American Airlines, with the goal of expanding service to more destinations worldwide;
-- $100 million in improvements to the airline's terminal at New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport, including improved road access;
-- a refurbishment of the check-in area at London's Heathrow Airport;
-- expanded departure options from the United Kingdom, including the development of London's Gatwick Airport as a second hub.
British Airways U.S. stock fell $1 to $119.625 in late consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
